paper.title: The Non Catalytic Protein ERG28 has a Functional Role in Cholesterol Synthesis and is Coregulated Transcriptionally

assessor_text.text: The enzyme 7-dehydrocholesterol reductase (DHCR7) catalyzes the final step of cholesterol synthesis via the Kandutsch-Russell pathway, and is crucial in maintaining cellular cholesterol levels. Its absence leads to the devastating fetal developmental disorder Smith-Lemli-Opitz Syndrome (SLOS). How this enzyme is regulated has implications in controlling not only cholesterol synthesis, but also the synthesis of Vitamin D - another product of 7-dehydrocholesterol. In this study, we look specifically at how DHCR7 is regulated by the sterol regulatory element-binding protein-2 (SREBP-2) transcription factor. Sterol regulation has previously been studied in the rat DHCR7 promoter, but we have found that its regulatory elements are not all conserved in humans. Rather, the human promoter contains two binding sites for SREBP-2 (at -155 and -55) and a binding site for the nuclear factor-Y (NF-Y) cofactor (at -136). The -155 site is a particularly responsive sterol regulatory element (SRE) which is well conserved in mammals, and was possibly overlooked in the rat promoter study. The exact location of the weaker -55 site (close to the known rat SRE) may have shifted during evolution. Furthermore, we established that the two SREs that bind SREBP-2 work in cooperation to synergistically activate DHCR7. We have previously characterized the SREs in DHCR24, the final enzyme in the alternate Bloch pathway of cholesterol synthesis. Here, comparison of the sterol regulation of these terminal enzymes demonstrates the unique cooperative system that helps to control cholesterol synthesis.

paper.title: The sterol-based transcriptional control of human 7-dehydrocholesterol reductase (DHCR7): Evidence of a cooperative regulatory program in cholesterol synthesis

assessor_text.text:
Mammalian cells must maintain an intracellular reducing environment for survival (1). Reactive oxygen species (ROS) are generated as normal cellular metabolic byproducts (2), but an increase in ROS levels can induce oxidative stress that can lead to an inflammatory response (2). The thioredoxin system (thioredoxin/thioredoxin reductase/NADPH) is a crucial ubiquitous mechanism that protects against oxidative stress by its disulfide reductase function (3, 4, 5). The thioredoxin system is essential for mammals, as mice without thioredoxin-1 die shortly after implantation (6).

Thioredoxin-Interacting Protein (TXNIP) is a member of the arrestin domain–containing protein family (4, 7, 8). Members of this protein family, including TXNIP, play important roles in gluconeogenesis (9, 10, 11), adipogenesis (12), and fructose metabolism (13, 14). The absence of TXNIP can cause hyperlipidemia (15), hypoglycemia (11), decreased hepatic glucose production (HGP) (11), obesity (16), and increased beta cell survival (17). The TXNIP protein also participates in the regulation of peripheral glucose metabolism in humans (18). TXNIP is distinct from the other arrestin domain–containing proteins in its ability to bind to thioredoxin (4). TXNIP binds covalently to reduced thioredoxin and thus can inhibit thioredoxin disulfide reductase activity in vitro (19). TXNIP does not interact with oxidized thioredoxin or catalytic mutants of thioredoxin (4). The biochemistry of the TXNIP–thioredoxin bond is well characterized (4, 19, 20, 21). The key cysteine C247 of TXNIP is required for interaction with thioredoxin, as revealed by biochemistry and crystallography experiments (19, 20).

Transmembrane 7 Superfamily Member 2 (TM7SF2) is a transmembrane protein that resides in the endoplasmic reticulum and nuclear membranes and has C14-sterol reductase activity to assist the conversion of lanosterol to cholesterol in mammalian cells (22). In addition to its role in cholesterol biosynthesis, the Tm7sf2 gene can regulate insulin signaling (23, 24) and inflammation (25). In mice, Tm7sf2 was recently identified to be a tissue-specific nuclear envelope transmembrane protein that directs liver-specific patterns of radial genome organization for gene positioning (24). In addition to being a liver gene expression regulator, human TM7SF2 has also been shown to interact with an intracellular redox sensor protein in vitro (26).

The mechanism of diet-related insulin resistance is incompletely resolved. Improving diet-induced hepatic insulin resistance is a primary target for the cure of type 2 diabetes. Akt phosphorylation and consequent suppression of gluconeogenesis are central to the liver insulin response, but how hepatocyte signaling networks are dysregulated during a high-fat diet (HFD) and oxidative stress remains unclear. Increased oxidative stress has been extensively studied in metabolic diseases, including insulin resistance (27). Since TXNIP is molecularly positioned to sense redox potential and regulate metabolism, we explored the role of the unique redox-sensitive cysteine of TXNIP in mammalian metabolism. Our results show that mice with genetic editing of this single cysteine in TXNIP have altered lipid species profiles, increased hepatic insulin sensitivity and signaling, and decreased liver inflammation in the setting of an HFD. We also show that expression of Tm7sf2 is elevated in HFD-fed TXNIP C247S livers, and Tm7sf2 can regulate the insulin signaling pathway in liver cells under ROS-stress conditions, providing insight into the underlying mechanism of insulin resistance in hepatocytes during oxidative stress. We provide data that a cholesterol biosynthesis transmembrane protein plays an unexpected role in providing a missing link between oxidative state and hepatic insulin signaling. Together, our findings define a fundamental intersection between redox biology and mammalian hepatic metabolism.

We first sought insight into the role of the TXNIP–thioredoxin interaction in different organisms. Gathering data through available protein databases for TXNIP, we observed that the “..HIISGTCASW..” amino acid sequence that is known to bind human thioredoxin based on human TXNIP–thioredoxin coexpression studies (20) and includes the key C247 residue is only present in mammals (Fig. 1A). Most fish also bear a cysteine residue at approximately position 250 in a similar “..HIISGMCDMW..” amino acid sequence; it is currently unknown whether the piscine TXNIP binds thioredoxin. Other animal species we looked at, including members from reptile and amphibian classes, do not have this cysteine-containing motif, suggesting a selective pressure in mammals to retain the ability of TXNIP to bind to thioredoxin.Figure 1TXNIP C247 evolution and generation of TXNIP C247S mice.A, protein phylogenetic tree that shows the evolutionary history of the TXNIP protein. Species in yellow bear the cysteine residue at the 247 position and carry the “..HIISGTCASW..” sequence that is known to bind thioredoxin from the human TXNIP studies. Species in pink are from the fish family and except Latimeria Chalumnae bear a cysteine residue at ∼250 and carry a different “..HIISGMCDMW..” sequence with undefined ability to bind thioredoxin. B, TXNIP C247S mouse model strategy, (C) insulin (0.75 U/kg), (D) glucose (2 g/kg) (n = 9–10), and (E) pyruvate (2 g/kg) tolerance tests (n = 7–9) of 12-week-old WT, TXNIP C247S, and TXNIP KO mice. Data represented as mean ± standard deviation, one-way and two-way ANOVA with Tukey and Holm–Sidak post hoc tests were used, WT versus KO. ∗p < 0.05, ∗∗p < 0.005, ∗∗∗p < 0005, and ∗∗∗∗p < 0.00005. C247S, Cysteine 247 for Serine; TXNIP, Thioredoxin-Interacting Protein.

Data represented as mean ± standard deviation, one-way and two-way ANOVA with Tukey and Holm–Sidak post hoc tests were used, WT versus KO. ∗p < 0.05, ∗∗p < 0.005, ∗∗∗p < 0005, and ∗∗∗∗p < 0.00005. C247S, Cysteine 247 for Serine; TXNIP, Thioredoxin-Interacting Protein.

To evaluate the role of the TXNIP–thioredoxin interaction on in vivo metabolism, we generated a TXNIP C247S (or C247S) mouse model using the CRISPR–Cas9 technique. For the conversion of the cysteine 247 residue to serine, we mutated the TGC sequence to ATG in exon 5 (Fig. 1B). Cysteine and serine differ only in the exchange of a sulfur atom with oxygen; therefore, the amino acid position retains similar size while losing its redox sensitivity (28). The mutation was confirmed by both a new SpeI restriction site generated by the ATG mutation and Sanger sequencing (Fig. S1, A and B). We backcrossed the knock-in alleles for five generations to breed out potential off-target modifications and confirmed Mendelian ratios of allele inheritance. We also performed targeted locus amplification (TLA) sequencing to ensure the accurate integration of the mutated sequences into the native TXNIP loci, with no evidence of incorrect or off-target integration events (Fig. S1C). The pups appeared healthy, with a normal phenotype. We followed the body weights of the mice from 6 to 12 weeks of age and found no difference between groups by 12 weeks of age (Fig. S1D).

We performed insulin tolerance tests (ITTs), glucose tolerance tests (GTTs), and pyruvate tolerance tests (PTTs) on 12-week-old chow-fed WT, TXNIP C247S, and TXNIP KO mice. TXNIP KO mice were more insulin sensitive compared with WT mice as previously described (16), but we did not observe more insulin sensitivity in TXNIP C247S mice compared with WT mice (Fig. 1, C–E). We collected plasma samples from chow-fed WT, TXNIP C247S, and TXNIP KO mice after a 4-h fast to assess plasma lipid profiles. A hexosylceramide (d18:1/20:0) was measured to be lower in plasma of the TXNIP C247S group compared with the WT and TXNIP KO groups (Fig. 2A). Lysophosphatidylcholines (LPCs) are essential plasma lipids that control oxidative stress, NLR family pyrin domain–containing 3 (NLRP3)-mediated inflammation, and inflammatory markers such as tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNFα) (29). Low levels of plasma LPCs are positively correlated with type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and aging (30, 31, 32, 33). We observed that plasma levels of several LPC species were elevated in C247S mice compared with both WT and TXNIP KO groups (Fig. 2, B–F). We observed the following changes in C247S mice plasma LPC levels compared with WT mice: 23% increase for LPC 14:0, 37% increase for LPC 16:1, 23% increase for LPC 20:2, 45% increase for LPC 20:5, and 36% increase for LPC 22:5 species. Thus, despite similar glucose metabolism under a chow diet, we found substantial differences in the lipid profiles of TXNIP C247S mice compared with controls.Figure 2TXNIP C247S mice show increased insulin tolerance compared with WT mice following an HFD. Plasma (A) hexosylceramide (d18:1, 20:0), and (B–F) lysophosphatidylcholine species in 4-h fasted 12-week-old chow-fed WT, TXNIP C247S, and TXNIP KO mice (n = 5). G, insulin (1 U/kg), (H) glucose (1 g/kg), and (I) pyruvate (1 g/kg) tolerance test of TXNIP, C247S, and TXNIP KO mice that are on HFD for 8 weeks (n = 9–10). Data represented as mean ± standard deviation, one-way and two-way ANOVA with Tukey and Holm–Sidak post hoc tests were used, WT versus KO. ∗p < 0.05, ∗∗p < 0.005, ∗∗∗p < 0005, and ∗∗∗∗p < 0.00005. C247S, Cysteine 247 for Serine; HFD, high-fat diet; TXNIP, Thioredoxin-Interacting Protein.

G, insulin (1 U/kg), (H) glucose (1 g/kg), and (I) pyruvate (1 g/kg) tolerance test of TXNIP, C247S, and TXNIP KO mice that are on HFD for 8 weeks (n = 9–10). Since there were alterations in the lipid metabolism of TXNIP C247S mice, we placed these mice on a 60% HFD for 8 weeks to study their metabolic phenotypes under high fat–induced ROS-stress conditions. Following an HFD, TXNIP C247S mice had improved insulin tolerance compared with WT mice but did not have improved glucose or pyruvate tolerance (Fig. 2, G–I). As in controls, TXNIP KO mice also had elevated insulin sensitivity compared with WT mice as expected (16) (Fig. 2G).

To delineate the organs responsible for improved insulin sensitivity, we performed a standardized hyperinsulinemic–euglycemic clamp experiment with [3-3H]glucose infusion to assess whole-body glucose turnover and HGP and a bolus injection of [1–14C]2-deoxyglucose to measure insulin-stimulated glucose uptake in individual metabolic organs in 8-week HFD-fed mice. We and others have previously shown that TXNIP KO mice are more insulin sensitive compared with WT mice after an HFD (16, 34, 35). Both TXNIP C247S and TXNIP KO mice showed increased insulin sensitivity compared with the WT mice, and TXNIP KO mice were more insulin sensitive than TXNIP C247S mice based on the glucose infusion rates during insulin clamps (Fig. 3A). Whole-body glucose turnover rates were significantly elevated in both TXNIP C247S and TXNIP KO groups compared with WT controls (Fig. 3B). These findings demonstrate improved insulin sensitivity in the HFD-TXNIP C247S mice.Figure 3A single amino acid mutation in TXNIP protects mice from high-fat-induced hepatic insulin resistance compared with WT mice.A, whole-body glucose infusion rates, (B) whole-body glucose turnover rates, (C) hepatic insulin action, and (D) clamp hepatic glucose production rates during hyperinsulinemic–euglycemic clamp experiments of WT, TXNIP C247S, and TXNIP KO mice that are on HFD for 8 weeks (n = 7–10). E, plasma insulin levels of 5-h fasted WT, TXNIP C247S, and TXNIP KO mice that are on HFD for 8 weeks (n = 7–10). Hepatic insulin action, measured as insulin-mediated suppression of HGP, was increased significantly in the TXNIP C247S and TXNIP KO mice compared with WT controls after an HFD (Fig. 3C). This was due to a lower HGP during the insulin clamp, whereas basal HGP was not altered in these groups (15.9 mg/kg/m for WT, 20 mg/kg/m for TXNIP C247S, and 21.5 mg/kg/m for TXNIP KO groups), indicating the improved ability of insulin to inhibit gluconeogenesis in the livers of TXNIP C247S and TXNIP KO mice (Fig. 3D). These data pointed to the protection of TXNIP C247S mice from HFD-induced hepatic and whole-body insulin resistance because of the single amino acid mutation in TXNIP protein compared with WT mice. Five-hour fasted insulin levels tended to be higher in HFD-fed WT mice than in TXNIP C247S (p = 0.06) and TXNIP KO mice. The lower insulin levels in TXNIP KO mice were consistent with improved insulin sensitivity in these mice (Fig. 3E). In contrast, insulin-stimulated glucose uptake rates in white adipose tissue (epididymal) were similar in TXNIP C247S mice compared with WT mice (Fig. 3F). Also, only the TXNIP KO group had elevated skeletal muscle glucose uptake rates compared with WT mice (Fig. 3G). These results suggest that increased insulin sensitivity in the TXNIP C247S group was primarily because of protection from diet-induced hepatic insulin resistance. Despite significant changes in insulin resistance in TXNIP C247S mice, we did not observe any differences in TXNIP protein levels (Fig. S1E). We also did not detect a difference in oxidative stress marker GSH and GSH/GSSG ratios between WT and TXNIP C247S mice livers under chow diet where insulin sensitivities are similar between WT and TXNIP C247S groups (Fig. 3H). However, we noted lower GSH and GSH/GSSG values in HFD-fed TXNIP C247S livers compared with HFD-fed WT mice livers along with improved insulin sensitivity (Fig. 3I). There was no difference between groups for thioredoxin activity (Fig. S2A) between the TXNIP C247S group and WT group livers. There was no correlation between body weight and hepatic insulin action levels of the mice included in the hyperinsulinemic–euglycemic clamp studies (Fig. S2B). To confirm increased insulin signaling in the livers of TXNIP C247S mice, we performed Western blot analyses on insulin-stimulated tissues and detected increased Akt phosphorylation in the livers of the TXNIP C247S group compared with WT controls (Fig. 3J). These data suggest improved insulin signaling in the livers of HFD-fed TXNIP C247S mice. We did not observe a change in AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) or mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) phosphorylation in HFD-fed TXNIP C247S livers compared with HFD-fed WT livers (Fig. S2, C and D).

We measured liver free fatty acid levels in chow- and HFD-fed mice. We did not detect a difference between hepatic free fatty acid levels in the groups on a chow diet (Fig. S3A); however, the TXNIP C247S and TXNIP KO groups tended to have decreased hepatic free fatty acid levels compared with WT controls on an HFD (Fig. S3B). We did not detect a difference in the liver triglyceride levels between groups (Fig. S3C). Plasma beta-hydroxybutyrate levels were elevated in TXNIP KO mice compared with WT and TXNIP C247S groups under chow diet and HFD (Fig. S3D). Liver hexosylceramide (d18:1, 20:0) and LPC levels of the WT and TXNIP C247S mice were similar following an HFD (Fig. S3, E–J).

We then performed bulk RNA-Seq analysis to identify the altered genes and pathways in the TXNIP C247S and TXNIP KO livers under HFD conditions. The gene expression differences in the livers of TXNIP C247S and TXNIP KO mice compared with WT mice were surprisingly restricted given the metabolic phenotypes (Fig. 4, A–D). As Kyoto Encylopedia of Genes and Genomes database pathway analysis suggested, out of several genes that showed altered gene expression, the majority belonged to the cholesterol biosynthesis pathway (Fig. 5A). Genes that code for enzymes in the cholesterol synthesis pathway (Idi1, Fdps, Sqle, Cyp51, Tm7sf2, Nsdhl, Hsd7b17, and Dhcr7) were upregulated in the TXNIP C247S mouse livers compared with WT controls (Fig. 5B, the upregulated genes are highlighted in yellow boxes). We also validated the increased expressions of these cholesterol genes according to the RNA-Seq data in the TXNIP C247S group in a different cohort of mouse livers by quantitative PCR (Fig. 5C). The plasma total and free cholesterol levels were increased in mice by HFD (Fig. S3, L and M). One of the upregulated genes in TXNIP C247S mouse livers involved in cholesterol synthesis was particularly of interest. The Tm7sf2 gene codes for a protein that enables delta14-sterol reductase activity (22) and plays roles in several essential pathways. The TM7SF2 protein is a paralog of the Lamin-B receptor (LBR), which is also responsible for sterol reduction (24). This protein resides on nuclear and endoplasmic reticulum membranes (24). In the cholesterol biosynthesis pathway, the delta14-sterol reductase enzyme that the Tm7sf2 gene encodes can reduce C14-unsaturated sterols (36). The Tm7sf2 protein improves insulin sensitivity in mouse embryonic fibroblasts (23) and increases Akt phosphorylation in mouse livers (24), linking it to insulin signaling. Importantly, Tm7sf2 can control gene regulation in the liver, possibly through the protein’s ability to alter radial gene positioning within the nucleus (24). Moreover, Tm7sf2 controls the expression of several genes upstream and downstream in the cholesterol synthesis pathway (24). Because Tm7sf2 can affect both cholesterol biosynthesis and insulin sensitivity, we validated its upregulation by RT–quantitative PCR (qPCR) in a larger set of HFD-fed mouse livers (Fig. 5D).

Since Tm7sf2 was shown to alter Irs1/2 gene expression and positioning (24), we also tested for Irs1/2 mRNA expressions in mouse livers. Consistent with improved insulin signaling, we observed upregulated Irs2 mRNA expression in the HFD-fed TXNIP C247S mouse livers compared with WT and TXNIP KO mouse livers (Fig. 5E). On the other hand, we did not observe a significant difference in Irs1 mRNA expressions in the HFD-fed mouse livers (Fig. 5F). This finding agrees with prior studies that Irs2 plays a more dominant role in the liver and Irs1 in adipose tissue and skeletal muscles (37). Irs2 but not Irs1 is downregulated in the livers of subjects with metabolic dysfunction–associated steatohepatitis (38) and obese subjects with type 2 diabetes (39). Notably, the upregulation of Tm7sf2 and Irs2 mRNA expressions in the livers of the TXNIP C247S mice was present only under HFD conditions but not under the control chow diet (Fig. 5, E–H). The increase in Tm7sf2 and Irs2 mRNA expressions in TXNIP C247S mouse livers also corresponded to a downregulation in Pck1 mRNA (Fig. 5I), which is the downstream target of the Irs2 pathway in the liver and suppresses gluconeogenesis (37, 39). We also detected higher Srebp2 mRNA expression in HFD-fed TXNIP C247S livers compared with WT and TXNIP KO mice, which is the upstream regulator of Tm7sf2 (Fig. S3P). These findings reveal Tm7sf2 as a potential mediator of improved hepatic insulin action in the HFD-fed TXNIP C247S mice.

After identifying Tm7sf2 as the potential mediator of insulin signaling in the livers of TXNIP C247S mice, specifically under HFD conditions, we sought to investigate whether Tm7sf2 controls insulin signaling in human liver cells under ROS stress. For this purpose, we used human HEPG2 cells that were transfected with either a Tm7sf2 plasmid or an empty vector control plasmid to overexpress the Tm7sf2 gene (Fig. S3R). We treated the oxidative stress group with 100 μM H2O2 to induce oxidative stress and stimulated the cells with human insulin. We chose to use H2O2 and not DTT since 100 μM H2O2 does not affect WT TXNIP–thioredoxin binding as DTT does (19). We observed the same outcomes as the mouse livers in the human liver cell line after ROS stress. Akt phosphorylation was increased only in redox-stress conditions (H2O2) by Tm7sf2 overexpression in HEPG2 cells compared with the empty vector group and not under the nonstressed condition (Fig. 6, A and B). Irs2 mRNA expression seemed to show a strong increasing expression trend (p = 0.054, ANOVA with post hoc multiple comparison testing) by Tm7sf2 overexpression with the oxidative stress in the H2O2-stimulated cells (Fig. 6C). Irs1 mRNA expression also appeared to be downregulated by Tm7sf2 overexpression with the oxidative stress in the H2O2-stimulated cells (Fig. 6D). The mRNA expressions of gluconeogenesis downstream target genes of Akt pathway in the liver, Pck1 and G6Pase, were also downregulated in the Tm7sf2-overexpressing cells but only under oxidative stress conditions (Fig. 6, E and F). Protein levels of PCK1–PEPCK were also lower in the Tm7sf2-overexpressing cells only under oxidative stress conditions (Fig. 6, G and H). Tm7sf2 can also control an anti-inflammatory response, and deletion of Tm7sf2 results in NF-κB activation and TNFα upregulation (25). Therefore, we also studied the NF-κB pathway in the HFD-fed mouse livers. We found that phosphorylation of both IkappaB kinase (IKK) and NF-κB p65 was decreased in TXNIP C247S mouse livers compared with WT controls and that downstream PKC activity was also decreased (Fig. S4, A–C). In addition, the Tnfa mRNA expression increase observed in HFD-fed WT mouse livers did not occur in TXNIP C247S and TXNIP KO mice (Fig. S4D). We also observed a decrease in NLRP3 protein level in the livers of the TXNIP C247S group consuming the HFD, which did not occur in control groups (Fig. S4E).

Here, we also present clinical data of a family with some members carrying the heterozygous TXNIP C247S variant (Fig. 7A). The affected female patient was first evaluated in 2016 when she was 11 years old with a 2-year history of fever episodes accompanied by sore throat, abdominal pain, and headache. These symptoms largely disappeared over time. She presents normal body weight/body mass index value and normal plasma cholesterol and glucose levels. We obtained DNA from the patient and her parents for trio sequencing. The TXNIP C247S variant was inherited from her mother, who has a history of difficulty with weight loss and glucose intolerance. The mother presented abnormal weight, cholesterol, plasma glucose and blood pressure levels, which recovered following bariatric surgery. No other relative has been addressed regarding the C247S variant. The variant TXNIP (NM_006472.6):c.740G>C, p.(Cys247Ser), chr1:g.145994635C>G (hg38), is novel, with no previous documentation in population databases such as the 1000 Genomes Project, dbSNP, or the Genome Aggregation Database (gnomAD), version 4.1.0. Other variants of TXNIP C247 are observed in human databases. GnomAD, version 4.1.0 lists four other rare missense variants at the same codon: p.Cys247Trp (minor allele frequency [MAF]: 1.24e-6), p.Cys247Tyr (MAF: 6.20e-7), p.Cys247Gly (MAF: 1.24e-6), and p.Cys247Arg (MAF: 2.48e-6). Here, we show that the TXNIP–thioredoxin covalent interaction is necessary for developing HFD-induced hepatic insulin resistance. Among the altered cholesterol biosynthesis genes upregulated with the removal of the key C247 cysteine that allows the TXNIP–thioredoxin bond, the Tm7sf2 gene may play a key role in improving insulin signaling in mice and human liver cells (Fig. 7B). Furthermore, a heterozygous form of the TXNIP C247S variant appears well tolerated in humans. This suggests a specific evolutionarily conserved mechanism where redox state interacts with insulin resistance through this one specific cysteine in the TXNIP protein, presenting a key role. An HFD is known to induce ROS stress in organs, including the liver (40, 41), pancreas (42), intestines, and brain (43). While we did not observe a significant difference in glucose metabolism of TXNIP C247S mice compared with WT mice under a chow diet, the improved insulin sensitivity phenotype was clearly apparent after an HFD.

The TXNIP–thioredoxin interaction is important for diverse processes in mammals, including glucose metabolism and insulin signaling, inflammation, and mitochondrial metabolism (44). During the hyperinsulinemic–euglycemic assays, we assessed the insulin-stimulated glucose metabolism in liver, skeletal muscle, and white adipose tissues of the mice to define the major organ affected by the loss of TXNIP–thioredoxin interaction. According to results of hyperinsulinemic–euglycemic clamps, the liver was identified to be the main site that the increase in insulin sensitivity was mainly observed. We did not detect and increase in insulin sensitivity other major metabolic organs such as white adipose and skeletal muscle tissues.

The regulation of TXNIP activity is crucial for redox balance. However, TXNIP also regulates redox-independent physiological effects that directly influence pathophysiological processes, such as inflammatory responses, disrupted glucose metabolism, cellular senescence, and tumor development (21). Our laboratory has previously shown in vitro that TXNIP regulation of glucose uptake is independent of its interaction with thioredoxin. Also ARRDC4, a close homolog of TXNIP with a similar arrestin domain but does not interact with thioredoxin, also has the ability to inhibit glucose uptake (45). Therefore, it is possible that TXNIP might also regulate arrestin domain–dependent and redox-independent effects on glucose metabolism, potentially explaining the distinctive phenotypes observed in TXNIP C247S and TXNIP KO mice. Thioredoxin interaction is critical for redox-dependent functions of TXNIP (21). The structure of the thioredoxin–TXNIP complex shows that the interaction occurs through a redox-dependent disulfide bond switching mechanism. TXNIP C63 and C247 residues are also critical for TXNIP dimer formation (20). Even though the interaction is abolished with TXNIP C247S mutation, we did not observe a difference in thioredoxin activity levels in the liver after an HFD in TXNIP C247S or TXNIP KO groups, consistent with previous studies (11). This result suggests that TXNIP is not serving as a thioredoxin inhibitor in this setting; instead, TXNIP may be sensing the redox state and changing its molecular binding partners, as suggested by mass spectrometry experiments (46, 47). However, it is possible that the C247S mutation alters lipid and glucose metabolism by making more unbound thioredoxin available, even though we did not detect a difference in thioredoxin activity.

We found elevated Irs2 expression but not Irs1 expression in the HFD-fed TXNIP C247S livers. This finding agreed with selective downregulation of IRS2 during insulin resistance in metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver diseases (38). IRS2 plays a more critical role in insulin signaling in the liver than IRS1, which dominates in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue (37), particularly in the suppression of gluconeogenesis genes (38). Significant downregulation of hepatic IRS2 but not IRS1 expression in obese individuals with type 2 diabetes was also observed in comparison with nondiabetic obese patients (39). Our data agree with these studies, since Irs2 expression was increased and gluconeogenic signaling was decreased in TXNIP C247S livers.

The limited number of genes with expressions altered significantly with TXNIP C247S mutation suggests that this single amino acid mutation explicitly regulates the cholesterol biosynthesis pathway genes, including Tm7sf2, which also acts as a liver-specific gene positioner (24). The TM7SF2/NET47 protein is a member of a protein family that includes more than a hundred transmembrane proteins that reside on the nuclear envelope and that are constantly trafficked between the endoplasmic reticulum and nuclear membranes (48). TM7SF2 is preferentially expressed in the liver (48) to control both the position and expression of liver metabolism–specific genes (24). Interestingly, in Tm7sf2-KO mice, which have insulin sensitivity, only a set of 26 genes changed position and expression (24), which agrees with our limited number of altered genes.

We found that Tm7sf2 mRNA expression was elevated in the livers of C247S mice specifically under an HFD. TM7SF2 itself can bind NADPH and act as an oxidoreductase (49). TM7SF2 is predicted to be a part of a receptor complex (Alliance of Genome Resources), and previous research has shown that it can interact with the redox sensor protein HSCARG/NmrA like redox sensor 1 (NMRAL1) that also binds NADP (26). TM7SF2’s elevation in livers and liver cell lines, specifically under ROS stress, and interaction with oxidative stress sensors, suggests that it could be serving as a part of a redox-sensing receptor complex that links intracellular redox state to insulin signaling.

Although our results suggested a role for Tm7sf2 in regulating insulin signaling during oxidative stress in liver cells, with a molecular response correlating with findings in the TXNIP C247S mice, in the light of the current data we cannot determine causality between the Tm7sf2 expression and the TXNIP C247S phenotype. To causally link the Tmsf72 gene to TXNIP C247S phenotype in mice further in vivo glucose metabolism experiments should be performed in double-transgenic Tm7sf2 KO/TXNIP C247S mice in future studies.

Even though cholesterol biosynthesis genes were upregulated, we did not observe a significant difference in plasma and liver cholesterol levels in TXNIP C247S mice. Liver cholesterol synthesis fuels the essential supply of animal cell plasma membranes and is very responsive to dietary cholesterol intake (∼100-fold), which in turn controls plasma cholesterol levels (50, 51). Therefore, it was unsurprising to find unaltered plasma cholesterol levels in these mice. Furthermore, a total KO of the Tm7sf2 gene in mice did not impair cholesterol biosynthesis (52) even though it controls both upstream and downstream cholesterol biosynthesis genes (52). The reason that Tm7sf2 KO mice did not have altered cholesterol levels was suggested to be due to LBR protein with redundant functions (22). Tm7sf2 and lamin-B receptor (lbr) genes emerged through a gene duplication event (53), and they share the same C14-sterol reductase activity (54). It was shown that Tm7sf2 expression levels showed an opposite trend compared with that of lbr in livers (54, 55). Expression of one could thus increase to compensate for the decrease of the other. This could contribute to the similar liver cholesterol levels in our mouse groups. Furthermore, in HFD-fed mouse livers, cholesterol synthesis genes were found to be downregulated, whereas plasma cholesterol levels were elevated (56), suggesting that expression of hepatic cholesterol synthesis genes does not reflect peripheral cholesterol profiles. Also in our model, the lipid changes observed in circulation did not seem to have a significant direct effect on insulin sensitivity.

The TXNIP C247S mutation was also found to significantly benefit visual acuity during retinitis pigmentosa in mice (57). The activation of the insulin pathway is beneficial to retinitis pigmentosa cone survival (58), so improving insulin signaling by TXNIP C247S mutation could contribute to this amelioration of sight. In addition, our TXNIP C247S mutation was global. Although we primarily observed glucose effects in the liver, an HFD would also alter cytokine and hormone profiles in adipose tissue. We cannot exclude interorgan crosstalk as a potential factor in these experiments.

The evolutionary basis for insulin resistance has been intensely debated for decades (59, 60, 61). One concept is evolutionary mismatch, where genetic changes that were initially advantageous in some manner, lead to insulin resistance in the modern setting of a calorie-dense diet (59, 62, 63). We speculate that mammals may have retained the TXNIP interaction with reduced thioredoxin through TXNIP C247, whereas amphibians, reptiles, and other animal classes lost this interaction. It is interesting that fish may have retained a different cysteine motif nearby; however, it is not known if the cysteine of TXNIP in fish allows covalent binding with thioredoxin. In settings of infection or injury, oxidative stress could promote hepatic insulin resistance to increase energy availability (62). Insulin resistance also progresses much faster during rapid growth periods such as puberty, possibly to enable energy redistribution (64, 65, 66). Thus, the TXNIP–thioredoxin interaction could potentially represent a mechanism for the redistribution of energy in times of stress, with possible detrimental cost of hepatic insulin resistance in the setting of a calorie-dense diet.

We generated a new TXNIP C247S mouse model using CRISPR–Cas9 technology. Our strategy was to swap the TGC codon in exon 5 of TXNIP that codes for the key cysteine to an AGT serine codon, and this change also creates an SpeI digestion site (Figs. 1B, S1A). Injections of the zygotes were carried out by the Genome Modification Facility at Harvard University. Zygotic pronuclei were microinjected with purified Cas9 mRNA (100 ng/μl), in vitro–transcribed synthetic guide RNAs (Synthego), and an asymmetrical ssDNA donor construct (IDT). Microinjected zygotes were implanted into C57BL/6J surrogate females. Genotypes were confirmed by restriction enzyme digestion and Sanger sequencing (Fig. S1, A and B), and 100% mutated mice were used as colony founders. Selected mice were bred with WT C57BL/6J mice, and pups were genotyped to confirm that the desired C247S mutation was incorporated into the germline. TLA sequencing was performed by Cergentis on cells from the frozen bone marrow of TXNIP C247S and WT controls that were processed according to Cergentis' TLA protocol (67) to check for off-target mutations. This analysis aimed to identify breakpoint sequences of the genomic modification(s) and assess the presence of structural variants surrounding the TXNIP locus. No other sequence and structural variants were detected in the TXNIP gene locus chr3:96,557,957-96,561,857 other than the desired mutation (Fig. S1C). Before experiments, mice were backcrossed in a C57BL/6J genetic background for several generations. WT siblings from the TXNIP C247S colony backcrosses were used to generate WT control mice. TXNIP KO mice were previously created by our laboratory (68). Male mice were used for metabolic studies involving insulin sensitivity because of increased variability in females because of hormonal changes (69). All mice were housed at a controlled temperature and a light–dark cycle with free access to a standard chow diet (Prolab IsoPro RMH 3000 5P75; LabDiet) or 60% HFD (D12492i; Research Diets) and water.

Mice were fasted for 16 h before GTTs and PTTs and 4 h before ITTs. Fasted mice were injected intraperitoneally with glucose (1 or 2 g/kg), pyruvate (1 or 2 g/kg), or insulin (0.75 or 1 IU/kg) according to their diet. Blood samples were collected via the tail vein, and glucose levels were measured using a handheld glucometer (Contour) at designated time points. Insulin stimulation was performed by injecting insulin (1 U/kg) i.p. and collecting liver tissues after 10 min.

HEPG2 human liver cell lines from American Type Culture Collection were cultured with a complete growth medium with Eagle’s minimum essential medium. Cells were transfected with EV or Tm7sf2 vector (NET47 pEGFP-N2 [593] was a gift from Eric Schirmer, Addgene plasmid #61986) using Lipofectamine 3000 reagent (Thermo Fisher). After 48 h, cells were starved in serum-free Eagle’s minimal essential medium for 4 h and were stimulated with 100 μM 30% H2O2 during the last 2 h. Later, cells were stimulated with 10 nm human insulin for 10 min and then collected, and protein and RNA samples were isolated.

Insulin levels were measured in 4-h fasted plasma using ELISA kits according to the manufacturer's protocol (Alpco; #NH80-INSMSU-E01). Liver thioredoxin activity was measured in liver lysates in a sample buffer using a modified protocol from Cayman Chemicals. Liver free fatty acids were measured in chow and 8-week HFD-fed mouse livers using a Free-fatty-acid Assay Kit (Abcam; #ab65341). PKC activity was measured by PKC Kinase Activity Assay Kit in liver lysates (Abcam; #ab139437). The kit measures the activity of all PKC isoforms. Liver triglycerides were measured in 8-week HFD-fed mouse livers using a Triglyceride assay kit (Abcam; #ab65336). Plasma and liver total and free cholesterol levels were measured using a Cholesterol quantification kit (Sigma–Aldrich; #MAK043). Plasma beta hydroxybutyrate levels were measured using ketone body kits (Abcam; #ab83390, #ab272541). Liver GSH/GSSG values were measured using GSH/GSSG Ratio Detection Kit II (Abcam; #ab205811).

Western blots were performed using Phospho-Akt (Ser473) (#9271), Akt (#9272), Beta-actin (#8457), Phospho-IKKa/b (#2697), IKKb (#8943), Phospho-NFkB p65 (#3033), NFkB p65 (#8242), Pck1 (#12940S), NLRP3 (#15101S), AMPKa (D5A2) (#5831) p-AMPKa (#2535), p-mTOR (#5536), and mTOR (#2972) antibodies (Cell Signaling). Protein bands were detected using an enhanced chemiluminescence substrate. Images were taken either using an automated processor (Bio-Rad) or with autoradiography films that were exposed in cassettes in a darkroom. Antibody validation was based on our previous publications, and preliminary experiments and expected molecular weights were observed. ImageJ (US National Institutes of Health [NIH], https://imagej.net/ij/, 1997–2018) software was used to quantify western blot images.

Lipidomic analysis of plasma samples was performed as described by Su et al. (70). Briefly, after the addition of an internal standard mix, lipids were extracted from plasma samples using an adjusted methyl tery-butyl ether–methanol extraction (71). Extracted lipids were concentrated and reconstituted in a mixture of dichloromethane:methanol (50:50) containing 10 mM ammonium acetate before shotgun lipidomic analysis. Samples were directly infused into the mass spectrometer using a Shimadzu HPLC (Nexera LC-30AD). Separation and targeted profiling of lipid species was performed by combining differential mobility spectrometry and a QTRAP system (QTRAP 5500; SCIEX) run in multiple reaction monitoring mode. Data analysis and absolute quantification of lipids were conducted using the Shotgun Lipidomics Assistant, a Python-based application that facilitates differential mobility spectrometry–based lipidomics workflow (70).

Mice that were fed 8 weeks of HFD were sacrificed, and liver tissues were collected. RNA was isolated using QIAGEN RNeasy Kits. RNA samples were processed by Azenta Biosciences for library preparation and Bulk RNASeq reads (Illumina). Bioinformatic analysis was performed using raw FASTQ as follows: The reads were trimmed for quality and adapters with Trimmomatic v0.39 (72) with the following parameters: LEADING:3 TRAILING:3 SLIDINGWINDOW:4:15 MINLEN:36. The standard Kallisto index was retrieved from Pachter Lab’s Github (https://github.com/pachterlab/kallisto-transcriptome-indices). Sequence-based bias correction was performed using Kallisto v0.50.1 (73) with 100 bootstraps. The transcript-level abundances from Kallisto were summarized and imported into R as a matrix of counts using tximport v1.0.3 (74). Differentially expressed genes were determined by estimating fold change and dispersion using DESeq2 (75). Pseudogenes and mitochondrial genes, as identified by Ensembl (76), were first removed from the dataset. Subsequently, the remaining data were filtered based on a p value threshold of 0.05, followed by a two-tailed t test with a significance level of 0.05. These significant genes were visualized using pheatmap, v1.0.12 (77) and ggplot2 v3.4.4 (78). Pathway analysis was performed using pathfindR (79) (v2.4.1) using the Kyoto Encylopedia of Genes and Genomes database (80). Reactome and WikiPathways enrichment analysis was performed using Enrichr, using The Reactome Pathways Knowledgebase 2024 and WikiPathways 2024 Mouse database, respectively. Bar charts of the results were plotted using Matplotlib and Seaborn using Enrichr Appyter.

For verification of RNA-Seq results, gene expressions were measured by RT–qPCR in a different cohort of mice. For RT–qPCR, RNA was extracted from homogenized liver samples and cells by the TRIzol (Life Sciences) method according to the manufacturer's protocol. The complementary DNA was synthesized from 2 μg of total RNA by use of the High-Capacity cDNA synthesis kit (Applied Biosystems), and reactions were performed using the Taqman gene expression assays (#Mm00840455, #Mm00443258, #Mm01277042, #Mm00514571, #Mm00501703, #Mm03038438, #Mm00440636, #Mm01233546, #Mm00839336, #Mm01278327, #Mm01337454, #Mm00477897, #Mm0490968, #Mm00436772, #Mm03012094, #Mm01306292, #Hs02802676, #Hs00159918, #Hs00427620, #Hs00178563, #Hs00275843, #Hs00162807, #Hs01098079; Thermo Fisher).

To generate the protein phylogeny tree in Figure 1, orthologs were pulled from Ortho DB v11 (81), National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) database, and UniProt (82). The sequences were compared with NCBI COBALT (83), and iTOL and phyloT (84) software were used for tree generation.

Hyperinsulinemic–euglycemic clamp experiments were conducted at the UMass Metabolic Disease Research Center using a primed and continuous infusion of human insulin (2.5 mU/kg/min), and glucose was infused at variable rates to maintain euglycemia (69). Briefly, whole-body glucose turnover was measured using a continuous infusion of [3-3H] glucose during the clamp, and HGP was determined by subtracting the glucose infusion rate from the whole-body glucose turnover. At the end of the clamps, mice were anesthetized and individual tissues were taken for biochemical analysis (69).

Data were expressed as means ± STD. The significance of the difference in mean values was determined using one-way and two-way ANOVA with Tukey and Bonferroni, Holm–Sidak post hoc tests, and Kruskal–Wallis test with Benjamini, Krieger, and Yekutieli corrections and Student's t test where applicable. The statistical significance was set at a p value of <0.05.

All animal studies were performed in accordance with the NIH guidelines and approved by The Harvard Faculty of Arts and Sciences Standing Committee on the Use of Animals in Research (16-05-271/273). Patients were enrolled on NIH protocol 94-HG-0105 (NCT00001373). This study was approved by the “NIH Institutional Review Board” and complied with all relevant ethical regulations. Written and informed consent was obtained from all participants. Participants were not compensated for their participation. Human studies reported in the article abide by the Declaration of Helsinki principles.

paper.title: Covalent binding of thioredoxin to TXNIP is required for diet-induced insulin resistance in the liver

assessor_text.text:
BACKGROUND: Genetic inactivation and pharmacologic inhibition of the microsomal triglyceride transfer protein (MTP; gene name MTTP) inhibits hepatic secretion of VLDL, thereby reducing serum lipids and apoB at the expense of increasing hepatic steatosis.

AIM: To examine the effects of missense variants in MTTP on hepatic and circulating lipids.

METHODS: We analysed the association of MTTP missense variants with metabolic, hepatic and clinical phenotypes in the Penn Medicine Biobank (PMBB; n = 37,960) and the UKBiobank (UKB; n = 451,444).

RESULTS: We analysed 24 missense variants in MTTP in PMBB for association with biopsy-proven hepatic steatosis and found that an isoleucine 128 to threonine variant (I128T: rs3816873-A, frequency 26%) was associated with reduced steatosis (p < 0.001). PMBB subjects with imaging-proven steatosis also revealed significantly fewer carriers of MTTP I128T compared to controls. Analysis in UKB also showed that MTTP I128T was associated with reduced risk of hepatic steatosis. Unexpectedly, MTTP I128T was found to be associated with reduced plasma levels of LDL-cholesterol and apoB (all p < 0.001). Functional studies indicated that MTTP I128T is neither a classic loss nor gain of function allele.

CONCLUSIONS: MTTP I128T is associated with reduced hepatic steatosis as well as reduced plasma lipids and apoB. This paradoxical profile is not consistent with a simple gain or loss of function in MTP activity and suggests a more complex effect on MTP function. Further investigation of MTTP I128T will provide insight into the structure-function of MTP and potentially new approaches to modulate MTP activity that could both reduce hepatic and circulating lipids.

paper.title: A coding variant in the microsomal triglyceride transfer protein reduces both hepatic steatosis and plasma lipids

assessor_text.text:
Cholesterol is an important lipid for mammals, where it is required for cell membranes, lipid rafts, and bile acid and steroid hormone production (1). Its excess is linked to cardiovascular disease (2), and some cancers (3), while too little impairs embryonic development (4). Thus, cholesterol synthesis must be tightly regulated. The formation of cholesterol is energetically expensive, requiring abundant oxygen and cofactors such as NADPH in more than 20 enzymatic reactions. The two rate-limiting enzymes are 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA reductase (HMGCR) (5, 6), the target of the cholesterol-lowering drugs, statins, and squalene monooxygenase (SM) (7).

Flux is also controlled along the length of the pathway beyond the two established rate-limiting enzymes (8). This allows regulated accumulation of sterol intermediates, the importance of which is becoming increasingly appreciated. A growing list of studies implicate sterol intermediates in a range of biological functions from reversing cataracts (9) to suppressing protein aggregation and cytotoxicity in neurodegenerative disease states (10), to promoting oligodendrocyte formation (11), and even modulating immune function (12).

Post lanosterol, there are two parallel routes to cholesterol via the Bloch or Kandutsch-Russell pathways, where three methyl groups are removed from lanosterol to generate the 27-carbon frame of cholesterol. Lanosterol 14α demethylase (LDM) removes the methyl group at C14. Three enzymes then act sequentially in a functional complex to remove two methyl groups at C4, converting T-MAS (testis meiosis-activating sterol) to zymosterol (Fig. 1). First, SC4MOL (sterol-C4-methyl oxidase-like, also referred to by its gene name MSMO1) sequentially oxidizes one methyl group to produce a C4 carboxylic acid. Second, NSDHL (NAD(P)-dependent steroid dehydrogenase-like) catalyzes oxidative decarboxylation to yield a C3 keto-sterol product. Finally, HSD17B7 (hydroxysteroid 17-beta dehydrogenase) reduces the C3 ketone to produce the C4-demethylated sterol product. To remove both methyl groups from T-MAS for zymosterol production, two cycles of these reactions are required (13). The homologues in Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Erg25p, Erg26p, and Erg27p, respectively) are tethered together in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) by a scaffolding protein, Erg28p (14), and human ERG28 may play an analogous role in cholesterol synthesis (15).

Conversion of T-MAS to zymosterol catalyzed by SC4MOL, NSDHL, and HSD17B7 in the Bloch pathway. Two cycles of this reaction are required. C4-demethylation is circled in red.

Cholesterol levels are rapidly regulated by posttranslationally controlling the levels of biosynthetic enzymes through ER-associated degradation (ERAD) and the ubiquitin-proteasome system. In this system, an E3 ligase ubiquitinates substrates for proteasomal degradation and thereby depletes enzyme levels. Previous work found the early, rate-limiting enzymes HMGCR and SM are rapidly turned over in response to sterols and degraded by the proteasome (5, 6, 7). HMGCR is targeted by several E3 ubiquitin ligases (16, 17), including the E3 ligase, membrane-associated RING-CH-type finger 6 (MARCHF6), although SM is its canonical substrate (18). Moreover, MARCHF6 is an important regulator of cholesterol biosynthesis as it targets two other synthesis enzymes, LDM and 24-dehydrocholesterol reductase (DHCR24). LDM acts midway in the pathway, controlling entry into either the Bloch or Kandutsch-Russell pathway. DHCR24 can funnel intermediates from the Bloch to the Kandutsch-Russell pathway, in addition to performing the final step in the Bloch pathway to produce cholesterol from desmosterol (19). However, not all cholesterol synthesis enzymes are targeted by MARCHF6 for degradation; we have found 7-dehydrocholesterol reductase (DHCR7), 14-dehydrocholesterol reductase (DHCR14), lanosterol synthase, and 3-β-hydroxysteroid-Δ8,Δ7-isomerase are not MARCHF6 substrates (19, 20, 21).

MARCHF6 likely helps to coordinate the control of lipid metabolism (22) as it targets many cholesterol synthesis enzymes and other lipid metabolism proteins including perilipin-2 (23), a lipid droplet-binding protein, mutant variants of a bile salt pump, BSEP (24), and the cholesterol transporter NPC1 (25). Other MARCHF6 substrates include RGS2 (26), a G protein signaling protein; DIO2 (27), the main thyroid hormone activator; and DHX9 (28), an RNA helicase involved in thyroid cancer (28), suggesting a role in signaling and cancer. MARCHF6 mutations are linked with at least two neurological disorders. The chromosomal location of MARCHF6 maps to the cri-du-chat critical region, and TTTA/TTTCA repeat expansions in the first MARCHF6 intron are associated with familial adult myoclonic epilepsy (22, 29, 30). Recently, MARCHF6 was identified as an important regulator of ferroptosis, a form of cell death caused by iron-dependent lipid peroxidation modulated by the levels of the anabolic reductant NADPH (31). MARCHF6 promotes the degradation of ferroptosis effectors, p53, and acyl-CoA synthetase long-chain family member 4 (ACSL4). Moreover, NADPH binds to the evolutionarily conserved C terminus of MARCHF6, which is also involved in MARCHF6 substrate discrimination (31, 32). Consequently, MARCHF6 can act as an NADPH sensor to mediate cell death or survival (22, 31).

We hypothesized additional cholesterol synthesis enzymes are likely targeted by MARCHF6, in an elegant system evolved to rapidly shutdown the entire pathway at key steps. Here we sought to identify putative MARCHF6 substrates among the three enzymes comprising the C4-demethylation complex. In this study, using human and Chinese hamster ovary cell culture systems, we found SC4MOL is a MARCHF6 target, whereas NSDHL and HSD17B7 are not. We investigated the transcriptional and posttranslational regulation of SC4MOL and discovered it is rapidly turned over and sensitive to cell sterol levels. Furthermore, SC4MOL depletion results in a reduction in total cell cholesterol. Taken together, our findings support the concept that the initial enzyme in C4-demethylation, SC4MOL, is the most regulated step in this process.

Chinese hamster ovary 7 (CHO-7) cells (kind gifts of Drs Brown and Goldstein, University of Texas Southwestern) were grown in DMEM/F12 medium supplemented with 5% (v/v) lipoprotein-deficient serum (prepared from newborn calf serum in-house) and containing penicillin (100 U/ml) and streptomycin (100 μg/ml). CHO-7 cell lines stably expressing SC4MOL-V5 or NSDHL-V5 were generated with CHO-7 FRT cells as described previously (33) and grown in medium containing 100 μg/ml Hygromycin B. Huh7 and HEK293T cells were grown in DMEM/high glucose supplemented with 10% (v/v) fetal calf serum and penicillin (100 U/ml) and streptomycin (100 μg/ml). For HEK293T cells, plates were coated with polyethylenimine before seeding to ensure increased adherence.

Cells were seeded in 6-well or 12-well plates, transfected with siRNA or plasmids the following day, and/or treated as described in the figure legends.

The protein-coding sequences of NSDHL, SC4MOL, and HSD17B7 were amplified from HeLaT cDNA and cloned into our in-house pcDNA5/FRT construct (33) with a C-terminal V5 tag, with a CMV promoter. NSDHL was then moved to a construct with a weaker TK promoter to reduce expression levels. The pcDNA3.1-DHCR24-V5, pcDNA3.1-V5-DHCR24 (34), and pcDNA3.1-SM-V5 (7) were previously generated. NanoBiT® plasmids were cloned following the protocol outlined in the NanoBiT® PPI Starter System (Promega). SC4MOL NanoBiT® constructs were previously generated (15). SM-V5 (7) was amplified by PCR and subcloned using SacI and NheI restriction enzyme cloning into plasmids supplied in the kit [pBiT1.1-C (TK/LgBiT), pBiT2.1-C (TK/SmBiT), pBiT1.1-N (TK/LgBiT), or pBiT2.1-N (TK/SmBiT)]. MARCHF6-V5 (35) constructs were made similarly, but with NheI and EcoRI restriction enzymes. All plasmids were confirmed via Sanger sequencing conducted by the Ramaciotti Centre for Genomics at UNSW Sydney. Primer sequences are provided in supplemental Table S1.

Cells were seeded in 12-well plates and transfected with 25 nM siRNA [control (Sigma: SIC001-1NMOL), MARCHF6 (Sigma: SASI_Hs01_00105239), SC4MOL (Sigma: SASI_Hs01_00125914), NSDHL (Sigma: SASI_Hs01_00243652), ERG28 (SASI_Hs01_00143837)] using 2.5 μl Lipofectamine RNAiMAX (Life Technologies) for 24 h in media without antibiotics.

For plasmid transfections, HEK293T or Huh7 cells were seeded in 6-well or 12-well plates and transfected with 1 or 0.5 μg of plasmid, respectively, for 24 h, using Lipofectamine 3,000 as per manufacturer’s instructions.

Pretreatment and treatment media were DMEM/F12 media supplemented with 5% (v/v) lipoprotein-deficient serum, penicillin (100 U/ml) and streptomycin (100 μg/ml) and statin (compactin, 5 μM) and mevalonate (50 μM) to deplete cellular cholesterol.

For the Amplex Red assay, after siRNA transfection, Huh7 cells were washed once with PBS and refreshed with DMEM/high glucose supplemented with 10% (v/v) lipoprotein-deprived serum prepared in-house from fetal calf serum.

Cycloheximide (Sigma), MG132 (Sigma), and compactin (Sigma) were dissolved in DMSO. Mevalonate (Sigma) was dissolved in ethanol. Cholesterol-cyclodextrin (Sigma) was dissolved in filtered MilliQ water. Appropriate vehicle controls were used. Concentration of drugs used and treatment time are indicated in the figure legends.

Cells were seeded in triplicate wells and total RNA was extracted in Tri-Reagent. Superscript III reverse transcriptase (Invitrogen) was used for cDNA synthesis, following manufacturer’s instructions. Quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) was conducted using the QuantiNova Real-Time PCR kit (Qiagen), and gene expression levels of MARCHF6, SC4MOL, NSDHL, HSD17B7, and ERG28 were normalized to the housekeeping gene, porphobilinogen deaminase (PBGD), using the ΔΔCT method. mRNA levels of interest were normalized to the housekeeping gene PBGD and then normalized to the control, set to 1. Primer sequences are listed in supplemental Table S1.

Cells were lysed in RIPA buffer [20 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.4), 0.1% (w/v) SDS, 1% (w/v) IGEPAL CA-630, 0.5% (w/v) sodium deoxycholate, 150 mM NaCl, 5 mM EDTA, 1 mM sodium orthovanadate] supplemented with 2% (v/v) protease inhibitor cocktail (Sigma-Aldrich) and passed through a 23-gauge needle 20 times, rotated at 4°C for 30 min, and then centrifuged at 20,000 g at 4°C for 15 min. Protein concentration was measured using a Pierce Bicinchoninic Acid Protein Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) according to manufacturer’s instructions and normalized in lysis buffer with Laemmli buffer. Proteins were resolved by 10% (w/v) SDS-PAGE and transferred to nitrocellulose membranes (Bio-Rad). Membranes were blocked in 5% (w/v) skim milk in PBS with 1% Tween-20 (PBST) and incubated with the following primary antibodies: mouse anti-V5 tag (1:5,000; Life Technologies; R960-25), rabbit anti-SM (1:5,000; ProteinTech; 12544-1-AP), rabbit anti-vinculin (1:2,000; Abcam; ab129003), mouse anti-α-tubulin (1:10,000; Sigma-Aldrich; T5168). Following primary antibody incubation, membranes were incubated with HRP donkey anti-rabbit (1:10,000; Jackson ImmunoResearch Laboratories; 711-035-152) or donkey anti-mouse secondary antibodies (1:10,000 Jackson ImmunoResearch Laboratories; 715-035-150) for 1 h and imaged using the ImageQuant LAS 500 (GE Healthcare). All primary antibodies were diluted in 5% (w/v) bovine serum albumin in PBST and 0.02% (w/v) sodium azide. All secondary antibodies were diluted 1:10,000 in 5% (w/v) skim milk in PBST. Blots were washed with PBST for 3 × 10 min between blocking and antibody incubations. Full immunoblots for V5, vinculin, endogenous SM, and α-tubulin are shown in supplemental Fig. S1.

For NanoBiT® transfections, HEK293T cells in 12-well plates were cotransfected for 24 h with a total of 1,050 ng of plasmids, using Lipofectamine LTX as per manufacturer’s instructions. For MARCHF6 and SM constructs, 350 ng of plasmid containing the LgBiT or SmBiT tagged reporter construct was used, and for the lowly expressing SC4MOL, 700 ng of plasmid containing the LgBiT or SmBiT tagged reporter was used. Plasmid amounts were kept constant between conditions by addition of an empty vector. Corresponding HaloTag negative control plasmids were also used as per manufacturer’s instructions. After transfection, cells were split into a white opaque 96-well plate and left for 8 h to adhere.

Cells were then treated with 5 μM MG132 for 16 h. The medium was replaced with 50 μl serum-free Opti-MEM and incubated for 30 min at 37°C. A volume of 50 μl reagent mastermix (1 μl of Nano-Glo® Live Cell Substrate, 19 μl of Nano-Glo® LCS Dilution Buffer, and 30 μl of Opti-MEM per well) was added to each well. Luminescence was measured in a CLARIOstar microplate reader at 37°C, as per Promega’s instructions. Raw luciferase activity was normalized to the appropriate LgBiT:HaloTag negative control pair.

CHO-7 cells were cotransfected with 4 μg SC4MOL-V5, and 1 μg of V5-DHCR24 or DHCR24-V5 (34) in a 10-cm dish for 24 h. To prepare membranes for protease protection assays, cells were washed and scraped in PBS and centrifuged at 1,000 g for 5 min at 4°C. The pellet was resuspended in Buffer A [10 mM Hepes-KOH (pH 7.4), 10 mM KCl, 1.5 mM MgCl2, 5 mM sodium EDTA, 5 mM sodium EGTA, 250 mM sucrose] and passed through an 18-gauge needle 50 times. The cell lysate was centrifuged at 1,000 g for 5 min at 4°C. The supernatant was further centrifuged at 20,000 g for 15 min at 4°C. The resulting pellet (membrane fraction) was resuspended in 65 μl Buffer A.

Resuspended membranes were treated with 0, 0.02, 0.2, or 2 μg of trypsin in the presence or absence of 0.25% Triton X in Buffer A, for 30 min at 30°C. Loading buffer and heat inactivation at 95°C for 10 min stopped the reaction. Proteins were separated by SDS-PAGE and visualized by Western blotting.

The pcDNA5/FRT SC4MOL-V5 plasmid was used for megaprimer site-directed mutagenesis (36) to generate the K to R mutant plasmids. Primer sequences are listed in supplemental Table S1.

Cell cholesterol levels were measured using an Amplex™ Red Cholesterol Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Cells were washed three times with PBS, and 250 μl modified RIPA [50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 150 mM NaCl, 0.1% (w/v) SDS, 1.5% (w/v) IGEPAL CA-630, 0.5% (w/v) sodium deoxycholate, 2 mM MgCl2] supplemented with 2% (v/v) protease inhibitor cocktail (Sigma-Aldrich) was added to the wells. Cells were lysed by freeze-thawing from −80°C to room temperature. Lysates were rotated for 15 min at 4°C, and cellular debris was pelleted at 17,000 g for 15 min. Cell lysates were diluted 1:8 with modified RIPA. Amplex Red assay was conducted as per manufacturer’s instructions. Protein concentration was measured using a Pierce Bicinchoninic Acid Protein Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) according to manufacturer’s instructions. Total cholesterol content was normalized to protein content for each sample. Relative cholesterol content after siRNA knockdown was calculated by normalizing to the control, set to 1.

Multiple sequence alignment of SC4MOL protein sequence from human (UniProt: Q15800), macaque (Q4R4Q4), mouse (Q9CRA4), rat (O35532), pig (Q6UGB2), chicken (Q5ZLL6), zebrafish (Q7ZW77), and yeast Erg25 (P53045) was conducted in Geneious v11.0.4 with default settings. The complete human amino acid sequence of SC4MOL (Q15800) was used to predict membrane topology with TOPCONS (37).

For Western blot analysis, densitometry was conducted and normalized to the control in the first lane, set to 1.

To account for changes in basal protein expression in transient transfections and MARCHF6 knockdowns, we calculated MARCHF6 response of SC4MOL with respect to each transfected plasmid or siRNA condition, as described in previous work (38). Densitometry was first conducted, followed by normalization of the fold-increase for each construct after MARCHF6 siRNA knockdown to the fold-increase for WT, which was set to 1. A value close to 1 indicates the MARCHF6 response is similar to that of WT.

Images and densitometry were analyzed in LI-COR Image Studio Lite (Version 5.2). Graphs and statistical analyses were made with GraphPad Prism (Version 9.3.1).

We previously identified four cholesterol biosynthesis enzymes targeted by MARCHF6 (18, 22). Here we used a similar siRNA knockdown approach to identify if MARCHF6 targets any enzymes of the C4-demethylation complex, SC4MOL, NSDHL, and HSD17B7.

As an initial screen, we used siRNA to deplete MARCHF6 mRNA (Fig. 2A–C), then expressed our proteins of interest fused to a V5 epitope tag. The canonical substrate SM (18) was used as a positive control. We found an increase in SC4MOL levels after MARCHF6 knockdown, indicating that it is a putative MARCHF6 target (Fig. 2B, C). NSDHL and HSD17B7 levels did not increase, suggesting they are unlikely to be MARCHF6 substrates. Unexpectedly, NSDHL levels decreased after MARCHF6 knockdown. Thus, we generated stable CHO-7 cell lines expressing SC4MOL-V5 or NSDHL-V5 as a more robust and physiological system for detecting potential MARCHF6 substrates, as these express a single copy of the introduced gene per cell. In these cells, MARCHF6 was knocked down by >90% using siRNA (Fig. 2D, supplemental Fig. S2A), which resulted in a 2- to 3-fold increase in SC4MOL (Fig. 2E, F). We observed this result in seven independent clones (three clones shown in Fig. 2), providing further evidence MARCHF6 is involved in its turnover. By contrast, NSDHL-V5 levels did not change after MARCHF6 knockdown, suggesting NSDHL is not a MARCHF6 substrate (supplemental Fig. S2B, C).

SC4MOL is a likely MARCHF6 substrate. A–C, HEK293T cells were transfected with 25 nM control (−) or MARCHF6 (+) siRNA for 24 h, followed by transfection with the indicated plasmid for 24 h. A: MARCHF6 levels were measured using qRT-PCR and normalized to the housekeeping gene PBGD and control condition, which was set to 1 (represented by dashed line). B: Protein levels were measured by Western blotting with V5 and endogenous vinculin antibodies. C: Levels of each transfected protein after MARCHF6 siRNA knockdown were normalized to the control knockdown, set to 1 (represented by dashed line). D–F: Three clones of CHO-SC4MOL-V5 cells were transfected with 25 nM control (−) or MARCHF6 (+) siRNA for 24 h. D: MARCHF6 mRNA levels were measured using qRT-PCR and normalized to the housekeeping gene PBGD and to the control condition, which was set to 1 (represented by dashed line). E: Protein levels were analyzed by Western blotting with V5, endogenous SM, and α-tubulin antibodies. F: Relative protein levels were measured using ImageStudio Lite and normalized to the control condition, which was set to 1 (represented by dashed line). G: Schematic of NanoBiT® luciferase system for protein-protein interaction. 1) Proteins of interest (MARCHF6 and its interacting partners, SM or SC4MOL) are fused with LgBiT™ or SmBiT™ constructs. 2) If the proteins of interest interact with MARCHF6, a functional Nano Luciferase is formed, which acts on the NanoGlo substrate to produce luminescence. H: Relative luminosity is normalized to the response of the appropriate LgBiT:HaloTag negative control pair, set to 1 (represented by the dashed line). Data presented as mean ± SEM from n = 3 independent experiments performed in triplicates (A, D) or n = 3–4 experiments (C) or n = 3 experiments (F) or n = 3–4 independent experiments performed in duplicates (H), where ∗ P < 0.05, ∗∗P < 0.01. A paired Student’s two-tailed t test was conducted between control and MARCHF6 siRNA samples for each protein (A, C, D, and F) or the appropriate negative control and MARCHF6-interactor pair (H).

To further explore the interactions between MARCHF6 and SC4MOL, we used NanoLuc® Binary Technology (NanoBiT). This is a complementation assay where two proteins of interest are fused to complementary parts of a luciferase molecule, and if the proteins interact, functional luciferase is produced and luminescence can be measured (Fig. 2G). In our experience, we consistently observe low ectopic levels of both SC4MOL (Fig. 2A) and MARCHF6 (35). To improve the expression of SC4MOL and MARCHF6 NanoBiT constructs, and consequently luminescence signal, we treated cells with a proteasome inhibitor and successfully increased their levels (supplemental Fig. S3). As a positive control, we confirmed MARCHF6 and its canonical substrate SM interact in this system (Fig. 2H). Luminescence was produced by MARCHF6 and SC4MOL, regardless of whether the fusion was to the N or C terminus of the protein, consistent with MARCHF6 and SC4MOL interacting (Fig. 2H). Together with the siRNA data, these findings indicate that MARCHF6 targets SC4MOL.

To determine if SC4MOL is turned over by the ubiquitin-proteasome system, we treated our SC4MOL-V5 stable cells with a proteasome inhibitor, MG132. SC4MOL accumulated by 2- to 3-fold after proteasome inhibition (Fig. 3A), bolstering our observation that SC4MOL NanoBiT constructs were also stabilized upon MG132 addition (supplemental Fig. S3). Together, these data indicate SC4MOL is degraded by the proteasome.

SC4MOL is degraded by the proteasome, and MARCHF6 does not target lysines at SC4MOL’s C terminus. A: CHO-SC4MOL-V5 cells were treated with or without 10 μM MG132 for 8 h. B: Multiple sequence alignment of SC4MOL protein sequences from human, vertebrates, and yeast Erg25, conducted in Geneious v11.0.4. Residues with 100%, 99%–60% or <60% identity highlighted in black, gray, and white, respectively. Potential ubiquitinated lysines selected for site-directed mutagenesis are boxed in red. C–F: HEK293T cells were transfected with 25 nM control or MARCHF6 siRNA for 24 h, followed by transfection with wild type (WT), K284-291R or K284R SC4MOL mutant plasmids for 24 h. C: mRNA levels of MARCHF6 were measured using qRT-PCR and normalized to the housekeeping gene PBGD and control siRNA condition, which was set to 1 for each plasmid (represented by dashed line). D: Protein levels were analyzed by Western blotting with V5 (SC4MOL), endogenous SM and vinculin antibodies. E: Relative protein levels were measured using ImageStudio Lite and normalized to the control siRNA condition for each, which was set to 1 (represented by the dashed line). F: The fold increase for each SC4MOL construct after MARCHF6 siRNA knockdown was normalized to the fold increase for WT, which was set to 1 (represented by the dashed line). Data presented as mean ± SEM from n = 3 independent experiments each performed in triplicate (C) or from n = 3 independent experiments (E, F) where ∗P < 0.05, ∗∗P < 0.01. A paired Student’s two-tailed t test was conducted between control and MARCHF6 siRNA samples for wild-type and mutant samples.

PhosphoSitePlus (39) was examined to determine potential MARCHF6 ubiquitination sites on SC4MOL. K284 was the most likely candidate, with a total of 32 ubiquitination references recorded, including eight publications. PhosphositePlus also indicated K284 ubiquitination is conserved in mice, and a recent paper showed regulation in human SC4MOL at the K284 ubiquitination site by arsenite (40). K284 occurs in a lysine-rich stretch on the C terminus with proximal lysines at 286, 287, 290, and 291, although of these residues only K284 has been reported to be ubiquitinated (39). However, it is possible MARCHF6 may also ubiquitinate one or more of these adjacent lysines. Of note, K291 is conserved across all species examined, with the other lysines conserved in most vertebrate species (Fig. 3B).

To assist in our identification of SC4MOL’s ubiquitination sites, we considered whether these C-terminal lysines are exposed in the cytosol and therefore potentially positioned to be recognized by MARCHF6’s RING domain. The yeast homologue of MARCHF6, Doa10, recognizes cytosolic-facing regions of proteins (41), and MARCHF6 mediates proteasomal degradation of a soluble reporter protein at the cytosolic face of the ER membrane (42). We first examined the partial topology of SC4MOL. In silico predictions by TOPCONS (37) indicated conflicting topologies; four prediction programs suggested an ER luminal topology for the C terminus, while two programs predicted a cytosolic topology (supplemental Fig. S4A). To experimentally determine the orientation of the C terminus of SC4MOL, we conducted a protease protection assay with a C-terminal V5 epitope tag on SC4MOL expressed in HEK293T cells. Cytosolic portions of the protein are accessible to trypsin cleavage, while portions of the protein buried in the ER are not. We previously used this method to successfully map the topology of another cholesterogenic enzyme, DHCR24 (34), and therefore, DHCR24 constructs with V5 at the N terminus or C terminus were cotransfected with SC4MOL-V5. As published previously, DHCR24 results indicate a luminal N terminus and cytosolic C terminus. To ensure no DHCR24 trypsinized fragments are produced at the size of SC4MOL, a protease protection assay was conducted with DHCR24 constructs alone (supplemental Fig. S4B, C). Similar to DHCR24-V5, SC4MOL-V5 was digested by trypsin, indicating that the C terminus is trypsin accessible and therefore exposed in the cytosol and accessible to the MARCHF6 RING domain (supplemental Fig. S4D, E).

We used site-directed mutagenesis to make conservative lysine-to-arginine mutations at K284 and at all lysines between residues 284 and 291 (Fig. 3B). Although MARCHF6 was successfully knocked down in all cells (Fig. 3C), we found no blunting of the MARCHF6 response (Fig. 3D–F) for either mutant, suggesting MARCHF6 does not require these five C-terminal lysines of SC4MOL to promote its degradation.

We next examined the stability of SC4MOL protein by treating our stably expressing cells with the protein synthesis inhibitor cycloheximide for 8 h in medium containing statin and mevalonate. SC4MOL-V5 underwent significant degradation with less than 40% of the protein remaining for each of three clones (Fig. 4A, B). As clone 3 of SC4MOL had the greatest response to cycloheximide and MARCHF6 siRNA knockdown (Figs. 2E and 4A), it was selected for subsequent experiments.

SC4MOL is rapidly turned over. A, B: Three clones of CHO-SC4MOL-V5 were treated with or without 10 μg/ml cycloheximide (CHX) for 8 h. A: Protein levels were analyzed by Western blotting with V5, endogenous SM, and α-tubulin antibodies. B: Protein levels relative to the control condition for each clone, set to 1 (represented by dashed line). A Student’s paired two-tailed t test was conducted between the control and CHX (+) condition. C, D: CHO-SC4MOL-V5 cells were pretreated with 5 μM compactin and 50 μM mevalonate for 16 h and then treated with 10 μg/ml CHX for 0–8 h. C: Protein levels were analyzed by Western blotting with V5, endogenous SM, and α-tubulin antibodies. D: Protein levels are relative to the paired control for each time point, set to 1 for each protein (represented by dashed line). A paired Student’s two-tailed t test was conducted between CHX(−) and CHX(+) for each time point for SC4MOL-V5 and endogenous SM. B, D: All data are presented as mean ± SEM from n = 3 independent experiments each, where ∗P < 0.05, ∗∗P < 0.01.

As SC4MOL was highly turned over after 8 h, we performed a cycloheximide time course to measure its turnover rate. We found SC4MOL is rapidly turned over, with less than 50% remaining after 2 h of cycloheximide treatment (Fig. 4C, D). SC4MOL levels continued to decrease throughout the time course, with only ∼10% of protein remaining after 8 h of protein synthesis inhibition (Fig. 4C, D). Notably, NSDHL showed no turnover after 8 h (supplementary Fig. S5). Curiously, cholesterol depletion by statin treatment markedly increased SC4MOL levels over 8 h (Fig. 4C). This may indicate SC4MOL’s turnover is sensitive to cell sterol status.

Considering statin treatment increased SC4MOL protein levels (Fig. 4C), we next investigated whether SC4MOL is regulated in a similar manner to other cholesterol synthesis enzymes. SM, DHCR14, and DHCR7 (7, 20, 21) are degraded in the presence of cholesterol, while HMGCR’s degradation is triggered by oxysterols and other sterol intermediates (43).

Cells were pretreated with statin to decrease cell cholesterol levels and treated with cholesterol solubilized in methyl-β-cyclodextrin to increase cholesterol levels. Depleting cell cholesterol by statin treatment more than doubled SC4MOL-V5 levels after 8 h, suggesting the protein is very sensitive to cell cholesterol status (Fig. 5A). Treatment with cholesterol resulted in the degradation of SC4MOL after 8 h, with this decrease in protein levels seen under both conditions of normal cholesterol and cholesterol depletion (Fig. 5A). These findings indicate a high cholesterol status is a cue for SC4MOL protein turnover.

Sterols regulate SC4MOL transcriptionally and posttranslationally. Protein levels were analyzed by Western blotting with V5, endogenous SM, and α-tubulin antibodies. B: The maximum peak heights from four publicly available SREBP ChIP-seq databases on UCSC Genome browser (44, 45) were extracted (GM78 SREBP-2, HepG2 + insulin SREBP-1, HepG2 + pravastatin SREBP-1, and HepG2 + pravastatin SREBP-2). These were normalized to the peak height of LDLR in each set (represented by the dashed line) and then normalized peak heights were averaged across all four sets. SC4MOL, HSD17B7, and NSDHL are indicated in red. A Student’s two-tailed paired t test was conducted between the control and oxysterol treated conditions.
