To further explore the function of DDR2 in MASLD progression, 8-week-ol d C57BL/6J mice were given tail vein injections of Ad-shNC or Ad-shDDR2 (Fig. 7A). RT-qPCR and western blotting confirmed that Ad-shDDR2 significantly suppressed hepatic DDR2 expression (Fig. 7B and C). DDR2 silencing resulted in increased blood glucose levels relative to controls (Fig. 7D), and GTT results indicated markedly elevated glucose concentrations and area under the curve in Ad-shDDR2-injected mice, reflecting impaired glucose tolerance (Fig. 7E). However, after knockdown DDR2, there was no change in body weight or liver weight (Supplementary Fig. 5). Additionally, gluconeogenesis-related gene expression was markedly upregulated following DDR2 knockdown (Fig. 7F). Histological analysis using H&E staining indicated a modest increase in hepatic lipid deposition in the Ad-shDDR2 group compared to controls (Fig. 7G). Biochemical assays further demonstrated elevated hepatic TG and TC levels in mice treated with Ad-shDDR2 (Fig. 7H and I). Consistently, DDR2 knockdown markedly elevated hepatic mRNA levels of genes involved in lipogenesis (Fig. 7J), while protein levels of Srebp-1c, Fasn, and Acc were also elevated (Fig. 7K). Conversely, phosphorylation levels of AMPK and ACC were notably reduced (Fig. 7L), suggesting that DDR2 deficiency promotes hepatic lipid synthesis, thereby exacerbating hepatic steatosis.

MASLD is defined by abnormal fat accumulation in the liver (hepatic steatosis) and commonly linked to hepatic IR26. IR results in elevated circulating insulin levels, which drive hepatic lipid synthesis by stimulation of insulin-sensitive pathways that increase the levels and activities of SREBP-1c and various enzymes involved in lipogenesis27. Metabolic dysfunction in hepatocytes and impaired insulin signaling increase TG storage and create an imbalance between fatty acid uptake and output, leading to hepatic steatosis28. The prevalence of MASLD continues to rise due to increasing rates of obesity, IR, and hyperlipidemia29.

This study found that hepatic DDR2 protein level was reduced in both db/db and HFD-fed mice relative to the controls. The DDR family is known to regulate immune functions and cellular morphology30, with different forms of DDRs promoting unique protein synthesis and growth processes during cellular development31. The human DDR2 gene alterations have been linked to rare conditions such as dwarfism, spondylo-meta-epiphyseal dysplasia (SMED), and short limb-hand syndrome32. It has been indicated that DDR2 transgenic mice exhibit increased leptin production, leading to reduced epididymal fat, suggesting that DDR2 may regulate fat metabolism, absorption, and storage22. Nevertheless, DDR2’s function in lipid metabolism remains incompletely understood. Herein, our in vitro and in vivo experiments demonstrated that DDR2 overexpression reduces TG accumulation in hepatocytes. The findings indicate that DDR2 serves as a critical factor in mitigating lipid synthesis, ER stress, and inflammation in mouse liver cells in both cellular and animal models. Conversely, DDR2 deficiency aggravated lipid accumulation in the liver. These discoveries suggest that DDR2 may be a candidate modulator for MASLD. It should be noted that in our in vitro experiments we used primary mouse hepatocytes. Under physiological conditions these cells are not a major source of collagen; they express and secrete only minimal amounts of collagen under specific stimuli33. In the normal liver, collagen synthesis is carried out almost exclusively by hepatic stellate cells, whereas hepatocytes contain virtually no detectable collagen mRNA or protein. We therefore consider that the observed regulation of lipid metabolism in vitro is likely attributable to DDR2 itself, independently of exogenous collagen. Previous research has demonstrated elevated DDR2 expression in HCC compared to non-HCC tissues, primarily resulting from hepatitis B virus infection, with DDR2 significantly facilitating HCC invasion and metastasis34, however, there is a significant difference compared to fatty liver conditions associated with high fat intake or obesity.

AMPK activation plays a vital role in various metabolic improvements, with many proposed MASLD treatment regimens incorporating the activation of this cellular energy-sensing enzyme35,36 In hepatocytes, decreased AMPK activity reduces ACC phosphorylation, leading to diminished fatty acid oxidation and increased lipogenesis36,37. In addition to ACC inhibition, activated AMPK has been reported to suppress fat synthesis via the Srebp-1c/Fasn/Scd1 signaling pathway38, and it also downregulates Srebp-1c expression39, a key factor in hepatic modulation of DNL genes. This study demonstrated that DDR2 overexpression, both in vitro and in vivo, enhanced phosphorylation of AMPK and ACC. Increased DDR2 levels also diminished the levels of key de novo lipogenesis (DNL) genes, while reducing triglyceride (TG) accumulation in hepatocytes. In contrast, DDR2 silencing resulted in reduced AMPK and ACC phosphorylation, accompanied by elevated expression of key de novo lipogenesis (DNL) genes, thereby promoting lipid synthesis in hepatocytes. Additionally, DDR2 upregulation in db/db and HFD-fed mice led to lowered blood glucose levels and downregulation of gluconeogenesis-related genes (PEPCK and Pgc-1α). Although it has been reported that Pgc-1α does not affect lipid pathway40, however, AMPK as an upstream regulator of Pgc-1α, which plays a key role in regulating glucose metabolism41. These outcomes align with earlier reports indicating that AMPK activation contributes to reduced levels of blood glucose and genes involved in gluconeogenesis in obese mice42. Although DDR2 influenced glucose tolerance in mice, it did not significantly affect insulin sensitivity. We therefore propose that DDR2 represses gluconeogenic genes indirectly, in a non-cell-autonomous manner, most likely by modulating systemic insulin sensitivity and/or the hepatic lipid milieu.

To verify the involvement of the AMPK/ACC pathway in DDR2-mediated effects, this study utilized compound C and A769662 to modulate the pathway. Compound C, an inhibitor of AMPK, reversed DDR2 activation of AMPK and ACC activity, whereas the AMPK activator A769662 counteracted the suppression of AMPK and ACC following DDR2 knockdown. These results indicate that DDR2 helps mitigate hepatic steatosis and maintain lipid metabolism homeostasis by enhancing ACC phosphorylation through AMPK activation. RNA-seq analysis further confirmed that DDR2 overexpression is associated with enrichment in the AMPK signaling pathway. Previous studies have highlighted the pivotal function of ER stress and inflammation in the progression of fatty liver disease and NASH43,44. ER stress triggered by excess lipid accumulation activates the unfolded protein response, which promotes hepatocyte inflammation, oxidative stress, and cell death. Inflammation, involving Kupffer cells and pro-inflammatory cytokines amplifies hepatic injury and drives progression from steatosis to NASH. This study demonstrated that DDR2 upregulation alleviates tunicamycin- and HFD-induced ER stress in hepatocytes and ameliorates hepatic inflammatory responses in mice. In fact, earlier findings have shown that the deletion of DDR2 in myeloid cells can exacerbates inflammation in obese mice induced by HFD45, indicating the protective role of DDR2 against inflammation. These findings suggest that increased DDR2 levels can attenuate ER stress and inflammation in the livers of db/db mice, thereby reducing the severity of fatty liver disease symptoms.

This study has some limitations. While it demonstrates that DDR2 regulates lipid metabolism in hepatocytes via modulation of AMPK activity, the precise molecular mechanisms underlying the intermolecular interactions remain unclear. Elucidating these non-canonical pathways which activate AMPK will be a priority in our follow-up investigations. At present we have only demonstrated metabolic improvement in 12-week HFD-fed or db/db mice; we have not verified the ability of DDR2 to reverse established fibrosis or long-standing MASH. Future studies should employ AAV8-DDR2-shRNA or inducible DDR2-KO models, extend the observation period to 24–30 weeks of HFD ± CCl4, and evaluate both fibrosis progression and systemic safety (heart/lung). Conditional knock-out or kinase-dead rescue experiments are still lacking, so we cannot distinguish whether the protective effects are attributable to DDR2 itself or to compensatory signaling triggered by overexpression. In addition, the present study shows that DDR2 suppresses gluconeogenic genes in vivo but not in isolated mouse primary hepatocytes, suggesting that this inhibitory effect is mediated by endocrine or inter-organ crosstalk that is absent in the in vitro setting. Furthermore, our in vitro validation has been limited to primary mouse hepatocytes and has not been extended to human hepatic cell lines. These all need further research.

In conclusion, this investigation provides evidence that DDR2 exerts a protective effect against MASLD pathogenesis. The findings indicate that DDR2 modulates hepatic lipid metabolism by inhibiting lipid synthesis, primarily through activation of the AMPK pathway. These results offer a potential molecular regulatory mechanism for MASLD progression and indicate that DDR2 represents a potential modulator worth further investigationa for addressing MASLD conditions.

Male ob/ob, db/m, db/db, and C57BL/6J mice (8–9 weeks old) were obtained from Gempharmatech Co., Ltd. (Nanjing, China), and were kept in a specific-pathogen-free environment at Anhui Medical University under a 12-hour light/dark cycle. Another group of 4-week-old C57BL/6J mice received unlimited access to regular chow (11.1% fat; Xietong Shengwu, XTI01WC-009, Jiangsu, China) or high-fat diet (HFD, 60% fat; SYSE BIO, PD6001, Changzhou, China) for 3 months, alongside freely available water. Adenoviral vectors were administered through tail vein injection of 200 µL of PBS with 0.75 × 10⁹ viral particles (vp)/mouse. Following a 6-hour fast conducted 11–14 days post-injection, liver tissues were harvested for subsequent biochemical evaluations. Mice were anesthetized by intraperitoneal injection of sodium pentobarbital (120 mg/kg) and euthanized by cervical dislocation. All experimental procedures were approved by the Ethics Committee of Anhui Medical University and were carried out in strict accordance with the ARRIVE guidelines. We further confirm that every experiment adhered to all applicable ethical regulations and standards.

Adenoviruses expressing mouse DDR2 with a C-terminal tag (Ad-DDR2, NM_022563.2) and control adenoviruses expressing GFP (Ad-GFP, #H201) were sourced from OBiO Technology (Shanghai, China). Recombinant adenoviruses for DDR2 knockdown (Ad-shDDR2) and controls targeting luciferase (Ad-shNC) were also produced by OBiO Technology. Purification of adenoviruses was conducted via cesium chloride density gradient centrifugation, and mice received injections of 7.5 × 1010 viral particles per mouse in 200 µL of saline.

After anesthetizing mice with 1% sodium pentobarbital (80 mg/kg) by intraperitoneal injection, the liver was exposed and the inferior vena cava and portal vein were isolated. Digestion of the liver by perfusion of collagenase II (gibco, 17101015) -containing perfusate after washing the liver of blood with perfusate from the inferior vena cava. After digestion is complete, centrifuge cells at 50 g, 4℃, 30 min (fixed angle) and discard the supernatant; the pellet represents primary parenchyma hepatocytes. Subsequently, cells were resuspended in RPMI 1640 medium supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum, 100 U/mL penicillin, and 0.1 mg/mL streptomycin, and maintained at 37 °C with 5% CO2. For adenoviral infection, 2.5 × 105 cells per well were placed into 6-well dishes and exposed to Ad-GFP, Ad-DDR2, Ad-shNC, or Ad-shDDR2. Cell lysates were procured 48–60 h after infection for subsequent analysis.

Total RNA was extracted from primary hepatocytes or tissue samples utilizing a TRIzol-based method (Invitrogen, Massachusetts, USA). After confirming RNA concentration and A260/280 ratio met requirements via NanoDrop analysis and reverse-transcribed to cDNA. RT-qPCR was executed utilizing SYBR Green (RK21203; Abclonal, Wuhan, China), with gene expression levels normalized to 36B4. The sequences of the primers are provided in Supplementary Table 1.

Cellular or tissue proteins were extracted utilizing RIPA buffer containing phosphatase and protease inhibitors. Proteins were resolved on 10% SDS-PAGE, succeeded by transfer onto polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) membranes. The membranes underwent overnight exposure to primary antibodies (Supplementary Table 2) at 4 °C, succeeded by treatment with peroxidase-linked secondary antibodies (dilution 1:10,000, Jackson Immuno Research Laboratories, PA, USA).

For Oil Red O staining, a mixture containing 30 mM glucose plus 100 nM insulin (I0305000; Sigma, Missouri, USA), combined with 10% BSA, underwent dilution in medium to the desired levels. Dilute the 0.5% oil-red-O (O0625; Sigma) staining stock solution with isopropanol to prepare a 60% concentration oil red working solution, then stain the cells for 10 min to examine the amount of lipid accumulation. The measurement of intracellular TG levels was performed with a TG Content Assay Kit (E1013; Applygen, Beijing, China) per the supplier’s protocols.

The glucose tolerance test (GTT) required animals to undergo a 16-hour fasting period prior to receiving glucose through intraperitoneal administration at 1 g/kg. Blood glucose levels were measured at 0, 15, 30, 45, 60, 90, and 120 min by collecting whole blood from the tail vein.

During histological examination, the liver specimens were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde, followed by paraffin-embedding, sectioning (4–6 μm), and staining with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E). Regarding Oil Red O staining, hepatic tissue specimens in frozen state were cut to 8–10 μm thickness and subsequently treated with Oil Red O and hematoxylin. Immunohistochemical analysis was executed to examine F4/80 expression within liver specimens. To prepare samples for transmission electron microscopy (TEM), liver tissue segments were subjected to fixation using 2.5% glutaraldehyde over 12 h, then sectioned into 70 nm slices for lead staining. This section was prepared by Anhui Xinle Company.

Serum TG and glucose measurements were executed utilizing an automated analyzer (Monach) in the clinical laboratories of the First Affiliated Hospital of Anhui Medical University, Hefei, China. Serum TNF-α levels were ascertained through an ELISA kit (E-MSEL-M0002, Elabscience Biotechnology Inc., Wuhan, China).

Hepatic TG and total cholesterol (TC) content were quantified via enzymatic assays as specified by the manufacturer (Applygen Technologies, E1013 for TG and E1015 for TC). Absorbance at 570 nm was recorded utilizing a microporous plate spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA).

BGI Genomics (Shenzhen, China) conducted the transcriptome sequencing and subsequent analysis. The extraction of total RNA utilized TRIzol reagent following a 24-hour exposure of mouse primary hepatocytes to Ad-GFP or Ad-DDR2. Efficient mRNA reverse transcription and amplification were completed using the DNBelab C-Series platform, followed by single-cell transcriptome library sequencing on the DNBSEQ high-throughput platform. The RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) datasets were submitted to NCBI and are accessible under SRA accession number PRJNA1171978. Subsequently, we performed Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) analysis on the differentially expressed genes to further investigate the signaling pathways involved in their regulation. This KEGG analysis has been authorized by Kanehisa Laboratories46–48.

Statistical analyses were executed utilizing GraphPad Prism version 8.0. Data are presented as the mean ± SEM from a minimum of three independent experiments. For pairwise comparisons, Student’s t-test was used as pre-specified, and no additional post hoc tests were applied. Statistical analyses were performed using 2-way ANOVA to compare differences among the four groups. When overall significance was observed, Tukey’s post hoc test was applied for multiple pairwise comparisons; with group differences shown as * (or #) P < 0.05, ** (or ##) P < 0.01, and *** (or ###) P < 0.001.

paper.title: DDR2 ameliorates nonalcoholic hepatic steatosis by activating the AMPK/ACC pathway

assessor_text.text: NS0 is a host cell line widely used for the production of recombinant therapeutic proteins. In this work, we investigated the cholesterol-dependent phenotype of NS0 cells. Growth response to different precursors and comparative transcript analyses pointed to deficiency of 17beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 7 (Hsd17b7) in NS0 cells. Hsd17b7 was previously shown to encode for an enzyme involved in estrogenic steroid biosynthesis. Its recent cloning into a yeast mutant deficient in ERG27 led to its functional characterization as the 3-ketoreductase of the cholesterol biosynthesis pathway. To ascertain that its cholesterol biosynthesis is blocked at the reduction reaction catalyzed by Hsd17b7, we genetically engineered NS0 cells to over express Hsd17b7. The stable transfectants of Hsd17b7 were able to grow independent of cholesterol. The results affirm the role of Hsd17b7 in the cholesterol biosynthesis pathway in mammals. Further, the findings allow for rational engineering of this industrially important cell line to alleviate their cholesterol dependence.

assessor_text.text: The mevalonate-diphosphate decarboxylase (MVD) gene, a member of the mevalonate pathway, plays a critical role in regulating the biosynthesis of cholesterol, steroid hormones, and non-steroid isoprenoids. Previous studies have suggested that the MVD c.746 T > C mutation is a major pathogenic gene of porokeratosis (PK), an autoinflammatory keratinization disease (AIKD) with unclear pathogenesis, few effective treatments, and no suitable animal model. To investigate the function of MvdF250S/+ mutation, we developed a novel MvdF250S/+ mouse model carrying an equivalent point mutation to the most common genetic variation among Chinese PK patients (MVDF249S/+) using CRISPR/Cas9 technology, which exhibited reduced cutaneous expression of Mvd protein. In the absence of external stimulation, MvdF250S/+ mice did not display specific phenotypes. However, upon induction with imiquimod (IMQ), MvdF250S/+ mice exhibited decreased susceptibility to skin acute inflammation compared to wild-type (WT) mice, as evidenced by reduced cutaneous proliferation and lower protein levels of IL-17a and IL-1β. Additionally, after IMQ induction, the MvdF250S/+mice exhibited downregulated collagen generation and upregulated expression of Fabp3 compared to WT mice, whereas no significant changes in the key genes related to cholesterol regulation were found. Furthermore, the MvdF250S/+ mutation activated autophagy. Our findings provided insights into the biological function of MVD in the skin.

paper.title: Decreased Imiquimod-Induced Psoriasis-Like Skin Inflammation in a Novel MvdF250S/+ Knock-In Mouse Model
